lines.note: Tsuikyaku means expulsion: the Japanese paraphrase oi ushinau and Portuguese botar fora both describe driving someone out. The opening continues the alphabetical sequence anticipated by the preceding page’s Tçui- catchword; it is a complete new entry, not a continuation of that catchword.
Desterrar completes the expulsion gloss with banishment. The small, worn vowel is read e in the Portuguese verb, correcting OCR deſtorrar without modernizing the printed long s.

runs.text: Primeiro dia da lũa, ou mes.

lines.note: Tsuitachi is the first day of the lunar month; the Portuguese gives the first day of the moon or month. The visible opening Tçu and internal itachi correct Içaitachi, which had also produced a misleading kana hint.
Tsuitachi shooji names a screen or partition: the Portuguese begins with a board or door. The headword’s caron in xǒji is visible and is retained as printed.

runs.text: beǒboſinho baixo, que poem como por antepa-

lines.note: The object is a low little screen placed as a barrier; antepa- continues as anteparo below. The worn Portuguese diminutive is provisionally read beǒboſinho from its surviving beǒb- and -ſinho types, replacing the incoherent hesboſinho; the small vowel after b is abraded. This is a Portuguese diminutive within the gloss, not a standalone Japanese example.

runs.text: ro do vento ao derredor do fogão da caſa.

lines.note: Ro completes anteparo: the low screen blocks wind around the household hearth. The line’s fogão and caſa specify the setting and finish the preceding object description.

Tsuite is glossed acerca, concerning or about; Rege datiuo describes the ni construction in the following example. The printed grammatical apparatus, including Vt, is italic; So- begins sore ni across the physical break.
Reni completes sore ni tsuite, concerning that, directly rendered Acerca dißo. The β-like double-s sort in dißo is retained rather than expanded to two modern letters.

runs.text: O matar, & deſtruir como por juſti-

lines.note: Tsuitoo here means killing or destroying under an act of justice, not the modern homophonous mourning term. The headword carries a caron and the Portuguese divides juſti- from ça on the next row.
Ça completes justiça; the alternative is action commanded by a lord. Dalgum ſenhor belongs to the authority for the punitive act, finishing the preceding definition.

Tsuishoo denotes flattery or ingratiating speech. The enlarged Portuguese type reads Liſonias with consonantal i, not the OCR’s j; the headword’s circumflex is distinct from the caron in the preceding entry. Tçui- starts a repeated example below.

The two alternatives are tsuishoo ni moosu and tsuishoo wo moosu, to speak flatteringly. The source visibly varies môſu and mǒſu, which is preserved; Liſõ- has an abbreviation tilde over o and continues as gear.
Gear completes Liſõgear, to flatter, followed by falar meiguices, saying ingratiating things. The initial fragment is Portuguese and must remain with the divided gloss above.

runs.text: Vaſo, ou outra obra de varios lauores

lines.note: Tsuishu is described as a vessel or other decorated object with various worked patterns. This wording supports a craft or lacquerwork sense without supplying a more specific material than the gloss establishes.

runs.text: com tintas, & molduras, que vem da China.

lines.note: Paints and moulded decoration complete the description, and the object is said to come from China. The whole row is Portuguese continuation, with its printed historical lauores and tintas preserved.
Tsuiyari are matching spears, defined as being the same size and form. The native initial has the T crossbar, correcting OCR Fçuiyari; fei- begins feitio across the row break.
Tio completes feitio, the spears’ form or construction. This short continuation closes the matching-spears entry and is not a separate item.

runs.text: Tçuiyaxi, ſu, ita. l, Tçuyaxi, ſu.

lines.note: Tsuiyashi, tsuiyasu, tsuiyaita and the shorter variant tsuyashi are supplied as principal forms for wasting or squandering. The recorded ita ending belongs to the historical paradigm; it is not modernized to shita.
Tar finishes gastar: spending badly or wasting. Takara wo tsuiyasu illustrates squandering one’s wealth; the Portuguese verb eſperdiçar keeps the source’s historical initial spelling.

runs.text: Tçuiye, uru, eta. l, Tçuye, uru.

lines.note: Tsuiye and the shorter tsuye are the intransitive counterparts, something being wasted or consumed. The first principal ending is visibly uru rather than OCR uſu; the Portuguese Eſperdi- continues on the next physical row.

runs.text: çarſe, ou gaſtarſe mal algua couſa. Vide

lines.note: Çarſe completes eſperdiçarſe, followed by wasting something badly. The printed algua is left without a supplied tilde because no secure mark remains; Vide introduces a cross-reference whose Tçu- continues below.
Ye, uru completes the cross-reference Tçuye, uru. This short roman continuation belongs to the named alternative form and is not a separate Portuguese gloss.
The noun tsuiye means expenditure, loss, or costs. The following Tçui- begins tsuiye ni naru, an example built from this noun rather than the preceding verbal principal forms.
Yeni naru completes tsuiye ni naru: to be or become a loss or expense. The Portuguese Ser, ou fazerſe explicitly distinguishes being from becoming.

Tsuizen is a memorial or commendation for a deceased person. The continuous defũto has a visible f and a tilde abbreviation over u; OCR de ſũto incorrectly separated the word and confused f with long s. Saimẽto and comẽdação remain unexpanded.
Tsuuji, tsuuzuru, tsuujita means communicating or having passage. The first example begins kokoro wo tsuuzuru; the headword’s printed caron over u is preserved.

Corouo completes kokoro wo tsuuzuru; the Japanese paraphrase is kokorozashi wo kayowasu, exchanging intentions or sentiments. The x of Cocorozaxiuo is severely abraded: its surviving traces are compatible with x, and the morphology and following Portuguese support the chosen reading. This replaces the OCR comma, with the glyph-level doubt retained here.

Uaſu completes kayowasu. The Portuguese says that hearts and wishes communicate or agree; the printed Communicarenſe is retained with n before ſe rather than silently adjusted to a modern -m spelling.

Hearts and intentions complete the preceding communication gloss. Inshin wo tsuuzuru begins a new example of exchanging presents; the worn but visible u and caron correct OCR tçôzu-, and the Portuguese plural is read corações.

runs.text: Mandar preſentes entre ſi, ou de hua ſô

lines.note: Ru completes tsuuzuru. The gloss describes sending presents mutually or from only one side; preſentes corrects the OCR vowel, and the final ſô belongs entirely to the italic Portuguese phrase continuing below.

Parte finishes the presents coming from one side. Kuchi ga tsuuzuru then means understanding one another in speech. A fresh enlarged comparison shows two feet and one arch in the final n, so en- replaces OCR em- and continues into entreſi; the faint u accent is read as a caron.

runs.text: treſi no falar. ¶ Item, Fazer ſuas neceßida-

lines.note: Treſi completes en-treſi no falar, mutual understanding when speaking. Item introduces another sense, freely passing bodily waste; the scan has Item and a single β-like double-s sort in neceßida-, correcting the OCR’s extra letters.
Des completes neceßidades; Daiben or Xôben supplies defecation or urination as the example. These Japanese nouns share the following predicate and are not separate glossed entries here.

The first tsuuzuru completes the daiben/xooben example and visibly carries a circumflex, not the OCR tilde. Ri ga tsuuzuru introduces a related bowel-passage example with a caron over u; ca- begins the Portuguese camara.
Mara completes fazer camara, here bowel evacuation, with liuremente and sem impedimento specifying unobstructed passage. It closes the bodily-function sense of the verb above.
Tsuuji and tsuuzzu are alternative names for an interpreter. The repeated z in Tçǔzzu and the carons are printed distinctions, retained rather than normalized to one modern form.

The gloss and michi tsuji identify a crossroads. The headword is read Tçǔji from the surviving T, ç, u accent, and ji types, correcting OCR Teǔ,i; its long-vowel mark is kept despite the familiar short-vowel tsuji reading. Portuguese Encruzilhada is visible, not Encrazilhada.

Atama no tsuji names the crown or top of the head, glossed Cucuruta da cabeça. The source leaves no secure full stop between the Japanese phrase and its italic gloss; one is not supplied for consistency.
Tsujikaze is a whirlwind, directly matched by Redemoinho de vento. The intervocalic j and the source’s caje spelling are retained as printed.

runs.text: Lanterna que ſe poem em alto nas

lines.note: Tsujidooro is a lantern set high at crossroads, with the location completed below. A small damaged mark over the first o is read as a caron from its downward remnant; the NINJAL lexical index instead supplies ô, so this chosen graphic reading remains uncertain and does not silently import the index’s spelling.
Encruzilhadas supplies the location where the lantern is raised. The native row supports n and c after e, correcting OCR eneruzilhadas and completing the preceding entry.
Tsujigahana is explained as a painted katabira garment. Catabira is a Japanese garment-name embedded in Portuguese explanatory prose; the following lines describe its decorative foliage and colours.

runs.text: lhagens, lauores vermelhos, & de outras co-

lines.note: Lhagens completes folhagens, the foliage designs, followed by red decoration and other colours. The physical co- is the beginning of cores below, not an independent abbreviation.

runs.text: res. ¶ Itẽ, os meſmos lauores, ou pinturas.

lines.note: Res completes cores. The added sense identifies the same decorative patterns or paintings themselves, widening the headword from the decorated garment to its ornamentation; the abbreviated Itẽ is retained.

runs.text: Guardas que ſe poem no cami-

lines.note: Tsuji gatame denotes guards posted along a route or at crossroads. The Portuguese cami- begins caminho, whose continuation explains the lord’s protection.

runs.text: nho pera vigia do ſenhor da Tenca, ou do Cu-

lines.note: Nho completes caminho: the guards watch for the lord of the Tenca or the Kuboo. The native text corrects nhe, ſenhoar, and Penca to nho, ſenhor, and Tenca; the Japanese title Cu- remains divided from bǒ on the next row.

Bǒ completes the title Cubǒ begun on the preceding row, followed by the printed &c. Enlarged comparison shows the tapered, sloping b and narrow o of the italic type, so the full fragment is italic. This genuine body continuation closes the first column and is not a catchword.

runs.text: Os que andão de noite matando nas

lines.note: Tsujigiri is glossed here as the people who roam at night killing at crossroads. The Portuguese Os que frames the term as agents or perpetrators, and the location continues on the next physical row.
Encruzilhadas completes the night-killing definition. The short Portuguese row belongs to tsujigiri and is separate from the following wind-name entry.

Tsujimaki is another term for a whirlwind. The faint leftmost T has a surviving top bar and starts at the same margin as neighboring headwords, so the missing initial and erroneous indentation are corrected. The terminal upright X. is the dictionary’s regional usage label.

runs.text: Caſa como oratorio, onde ſe ajũ-

lines.note: Tsujimoto first names a house or prayer-hall where people gather. Onde is visible rather than OCR ode, and ajũ- continues into ajuntão below with the abbreviation preserved.

runs.text: tão a fazer oração, &c. os Icòxus. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Tão completes the gathering for prayer by the Icòxus, the Ikkoo community named inside the Portuguese explanation. The first occurrence has a grave over o; the abbreviated Itẽ introduces the associated person sense on the following row.

runs.text: homem caſado que he como meſtre dos Icǒxus.

lines.note: The second sense is a married man acting as a master of the same religious community. Icǒxus has a clearly printed caron over o, differing from Icòxus above; this corrects OCR Ichxus while preserving the source’s variation.

Tsuji tsuji is the repeated form for crossroads, glossed with the Portuguese plural. The leftmost T is worn but retains its upper bar, correcting OCR Fçuji without changing the printed space between the repeated forms.

runs.text: Borda dalgũa couſa como do veſtido. Vt,

lines.note: Tsuma first means the edge or border of something such as clothing. Vt introduces examples of a garment’s edge and later a roof’s edge, rather than the spouse sense in the following separate entry.

Kirumono no tsuma is the edge of a garment, and tsuma wo kaitoru means gathering up its skirts. The visible m in Qirumonono and the worn final u of caitoru correct the OCR strings Qiruionono and caitorut.

runs.text: Tomar, ou aleuantar as fraldas do veſtido.

lines.note: The Portuguese explains taking or raising the garment’s skirts or hems. It translates the preceding tsuma wo kaitoru example, preserving the source spelling aleuantar.
Noki no tsuma names the edge of a roof. Borda do telhado extends the same edge sense beyond clothing while retaining the Japanese example as ordinary roman text.

runs.text: Eſpoſa, ou molher caſada. Item mi-

lines.note: This distinct tsuma entry means a wife or married woman. The visible cedilla corrects Tcuma; the Latin qualification mi- continues into minùs proprie, introducing a less proper application below.

runs.text: nùs proprie, Marido, ou homẽ caſado. ¶

lines.note: Nùs completes minùs proprie: husband or married man is listed as a less proper sense of tsuma. Tçu- then begins the example tsuma ni nasu, and the Portuguese homẽ abbreviation remains unexpanded.

runs.text: mani naſu. l, ſuru. l, ſadamuru.

lines.note: Mani completes tsuma ni; nasu, suru, and sadamuru are three alternative verbs for taking or settling on a wife. The row’s Ca- begins the Portuguese caſarſe, rather than a new Japanese form.
Sarſe completes caſarſe com algũa molher, to marry a woman. It finishes the three Japanese alternatives on the preceding row and preserves the printed tilde over u.

Tsuma barami denotes the nail condition glossed Vnheiro, a whitlow or swelling by the nail. The very faint initial T is recovered from its surviving bar at the headword margin; barami retains the source’s visible separation.
Tsumabirakana means clear or distinct, matching both Portuguese adjectives. The historical tsumabira- form is preserved rather than silently shortened to a familiar modern variant.
Tsumabirakani is the adverbial form, glossed Clara mente. The scan supports the visible separation of the Portuguese parts and the indented placement under the adjectival headword.

Tsumabirakasa supplies the corresponding abstract noun, clarity or distinctness, without a new Portuguese gloss. Its worn initial is T rather than OCR A; the indented physical row remains attached to the adjectival/adverbial group.
Tsumabukuro, alternatively kobukuro, is a little bag. The scan shows the long s in Bolſinha, omitted by OCR, and the abbreviated q̃ introduces the clause explaining its use by women.

runs.text: molheres metem varias couſas, como agu-

lines.note: Women put various things in the bag, with needles beginning as agu- at the right edge. This row continues the relative clause from em q̃ as, and the divided object is completed below.
Lhas completes agulhas, needles, followed by &c. The short row finishes the little-bag gloss and retains its separate physical-line identity.

runs.text: Porta eſtreita de engonços, ou de

lines.note: Tsumado is a narrow door with alternative ways of hanging or pivoting it. The first fitting is printed engonços, with o after g rather than OCR engenços; the next alternative continues below.
Couceira completes the alternative door fitting in the preceding gloss. It is Portuguese continuation and not another Japanese headword or an omitted standalone definition.
Tsumahajiki is a finger-flick or snap, rendered by paparote and caſtanheta. The Japanese f and j are the source’s historical spelling and are not modernized.
Tsumahajiki suru means making those flicks or snaps. The scan has the paragraph mark without the OCR’s following full stop, and the coordinated Portuguese gloss continues below.

Caſtanhetas completes the preceding finger-snap gloss. At this row’s far right the source also prints an opening parenthesis and vnhas.; these were omitted by OCR and are restored in their physical position. The displaced word supplies the object of faca de cortar in the next row, so it is not part of the caſtanhetas definition.

Tsumagatana is a small knife for cutting nails. The Portuguese visibly ends this row at cortar with no supplied continuation mark; the object vnhas. is printed at the far right of the preceding physical row and is preserved there as a displaced span.

Tsumage means tucking or lifting up one’s clothes. The headword’s damaged initial is T, and the Portuguese verb has a clear cedilla in Arregaçar, correcting OCR Fçumague and Arregagar while preserving historical forms.

The alternative gloss is raising the garment’s flaps or skirts. Two surviving strokes in the abraded gap after al support e in aleuantar, correcting OCR aluantar; the phrase completes the clothes-lifting entry.
Tsumagi means wood shavings or chips, glossed Maraualhas and cauacos. The example that follows shows gathering them as fuel, rather than identifying a particular tree.
Tsumagi wo hiroo means picking up those chips or little sticks. The printed firô has a circumflex and the Portuguese pao- continues into paozinhos below.
Zinhos completes paozinhos, little pieces of wood, and pera o fogo states their use as fuel. The source keeps pera rather than modern para.

Tsumagiwa, alternatively tsumane, is the root of a nail. The Japanese alternatives are ordinary headword material, while Raiz das vnhas supplies the anatomical gloss without altering the historical tsuma forms.

Tsumaguri gives the verb for passing beads through the hand. The native initial is T, and the final Portuguese word is polla with a, correcting OCR rçumaguri and pollu; the abbreviated principal forms u, utta are preserved.

runs.text: mão ao modo de quem reza por ellas. ¶

lines.note: The bead movement is done as by someone praying over them. Mão completes the preceding polla construction, and Ya- begins an additional example involving an arrow on the next row.

runs.text: Dar voltas à ſeta ſobre a

lines.note: Uo completes ya wo tsumaguru, turning an arrow. The Portuguese begins rotating the arrow over the thumbnail; the accent in à is preserved in the description of this motion.

runs.text: vnha do dedo polegar pera ver ſe eſtà torta, ou

lines.note: The arrow rests on the thumb’s nail so that one can see whether it is bent. The Portuguese eſtà retains its grave accent, and torta continues to the alternative direita below.
Direita completes the contrast between a bent and straight arrow. Ya wo tsumayoru is offered as an equivalent expression, with Idem pointing back to the same turning action.

runs.text: Certa eſpecie de carangrejos q̃ tem

lines.note: Tsumajiro first names a kind of crab with white claws, whose feature is completed below. The headword does not itself establish a modern species, and q̃ remains an unexpanded Portuguese abbreviation.

runs.text: as vnhas brancas. ¶ Item, Mãos brancas co-

lines.note: As vnhas brancas completes the crab’s white-claw description. Item adds white extremities or paws in animals; the divided co- begins a comparison to a dog on the next row.

Mo completes como de cão, white paws such as a dog’s. Kono inu wa tsu- begins the example completed below. The larger V and following italic t of the Vt label are retained in the baseline’s mixed type; the capital’s precise font classification remains a minor visual caveat.

runs.text: Eſte cão tem as mãos brancas.

lines.note: Majirogia completes tsumajiro ja: this dog has white paws. The Portuguese calls the paws mãos, a source-specific usage retained without replacing it with a modern anatomical word.

runs.text: ¶ Item, Hũa laya de mariſco como ameijoas.

lines.note: A third sense is a kind of shellfish resembling clams. The deliberately broad Hũa laya de mariſco como ameijoas does not warrant a more precise modern zoological identification.

runs.text: Paruo, ou tolo. Palaura que ſe

lines.note: Tsumamare means a fool or simpleton. The Portuguese begins an explanation of the word’s disparaging use rather than a neutral description of intelligence alone.

The word is said in contempt of servants or dependants; the printed ẽ abbreviation in ẽ deſprezo is visible and remains unexpanded. Tçu- begins a following Japanese equivalent across the physical row boundary.

Mamareta mono completes tsumamareta mono, a person characterized by the preceding insult. The worn narrow t has the same raised head and foot as eta in neighboring principal forms, rather than the broad bowl of c; this supports mamareta over OCR mamareca and agrees with the Japanese passive form.
